archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose play-by-play efficiency ranks near the top of the league but whose 5-4 record has been dragged down by giveaways, poor special teams and close losses, with the defense, not last year's offense, carrying it.

report.headline: A top-five team by efficiency, taxed by turnovers, special teams and close losses
report.take:
These Rams are not last year's Rams. The 2025 team won with the league's best net EPA and second-best offense, scoring 30.5 a game. This year's version scores 23.8 and wins with defense: fourth in EPA allowed, second against the deep ball, fourth on third downs. The net EPA still ranks fifth, so the quality is there. The style has flipped from McVay's offense-first teams to something closer to the 2020 group.

The gap between how well they play and what the standings show comes from three things. First, they give the ball away: 14 turnovers, two in most games, and a -4 differential. Second, special teams are costing them a lot, ranking 30th in EPA per game. Third, close games have broken the wrong way, most painfully the 18-16 home loss to Arizona as 12.5-point favorites. The point differential implies six wins rather than five, and winsOverExpected ranks 24th. That points to modest bad luck more than a flawed team.

The numbers hide two odd mismatches. The offensive line is elite: first in pressure rate allowed, first in stuff rate, 4.69 yards a carry. Yet the passing game ranks only 18th in EPA, with one of the slowest release times in the league, so Stafford holding the ball and those turnovers are leaking value the protection creates. On defense, the unit is excellent without a pass rush. It ranks 27th in pressure rate and 31st in QB hit rate, so it wins with coverage and tackling, keeping everything in front and taking away the deep ball.

That is why the injury report matters so much. The defense's formula runs through the secondary, and both Trent McDuffie (out) and Jaylen Watson (IR, likely for the season) are gone. Puka Nacua, who had 93 targets in seven games, is doubtful, and left guard Steve Avila may land on IR. The schedule after Arizona is brutal: Green Bay, Kansas City, at San Francisco, and two Seattle games. The Rams are good enough to make the playoffs, but the path just got harder.

strengths.title: Elite offensive line in both phases
strengths.body: The Rams allow pressure less often than anyone and get stuffed on runs less often than anyone, which keeps them on schedule and drives a top-five success rate. Kyren Williams and Blake Corum split the work behind it, so the run game doesn't hinge on one back. It has held all season, but Avila's hamstring injury threatens it directly.

strengths.title: A coverage defense that erases big plays
strengths.body: Without a real pass rush, this defense still ranks fourth in EPA allowed. It does it by taking away the deep ball, tackling well and getting off the field on third down. Its run defense ranks fourth in EPA allowed, so offenses can't simply lean on the ground. The catch is that the model depends on the corners, two of whom are now out.

strengths.title: Net efficiency ahead of the record
strengths.body: A net EPA ranked fifth, a top-eight scoring defense and the fourth-most yards per game describe a team that controls games. The record lags because of turnovers and special teams, not because the down-to-down play is poor. That kind of gap tends to close over a season.

concerns.title: Both starting outside corners are gone
concerns.body: McDuffie played 97% of snaps before going out, and Watson is on IR after shoulder surgery. For a defense ranked 27th in pressure rate, coverage was the whole plan. Backups now have to hold up without help from the rush. Slot receivers were already a soft spot, with opposing WR3s scoring well above their averages.

concerns.title: Giveaways and special teams bleed points
concerns.body: Fourteen turnovers against ten takeaways, plus a special teams unit ranked 30th in EPA per game, have turned games that efficiency says they should win into coin flips. The turnovers are partly a Stafford-holds-it tendency, given the 28th-ranked time to throw. They are also partly noise, and should ease somewhat. Special teams just lost long snapper Joe Cardona, which won't help.

concerns.title: Passing game under-delivers on great protection
concerns.body: Clean pockets should produce more than an 18th-ranked pass EPA. Last year this offense ranked second overall. The drop-off is real, and losing Nacua, by far the top target, makes it harder to fix soon.

trend.note: After the Week 6 home loss to Arizona, the Rams haven't lost, and the defense has allowed 21, 9 and 13 points in those wins. The offense has been uneven over the same stretch, so the upswing belongs mostly to the defense, and it now faces its secondary injuries.

nextGame.headline: Revenge spot against a gutted Arizona team with no pass defense
nextGame.body:
The Book has the Rams as 9.5-point road favorites with a low 40.5 total, and the matchup supports the side more than the points. Arizona's defense is last in the league in pass EPA allowed, 27th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed and has forced only seven takeaways. It is stout against the run, though, ranking eighth in rush EPA allowed. That points the Rams toward the air, the opposite of how they leaned in the 16-18 loss in Week 6. Arizona's offense ranks 20th in EPA. Its line, 27th in pressure rate allowed, is exactly what a Rams defense that rarely gets home can finally win against.

Availability tilts heavily toward Los Angeles. Arizona's Gardner Minshew, who started Week 9, is doubtful and reportedly faces season-ending elbow surgery. The receiving corps has lost Michael Wilson for the season and Kendrick Bourne to IR. The backfield is missing Jeremiyah Love, Bam Knight and James Conner, and center Hjalte Froholdt is in the concussion protocol. For the Rams, Nacua is doubtful, Avila is questionable and may go on IR, McDuffie is out, Watson is on IR, and Cardona's absence means a fill-in long snapper on a special teams unit that is already shaky.

waysToWin.title: Throw on the league's worst pass defense
waysToWin.body: Arizona allows the most EPA per dropback in the league and gets hurt both short and deep. Its WR2 coverage is among the worst by EPA per target, and tight ends have scored well above their averages against it. Even without Nacua, Davante Adams and the Higbee-Parkinson tight end pair have room. With Arizona's pass rush ranked 25th in pressure rate, Stafford should have time.

waysToWin.title: Smother a skeleton-crew offense
waysToWin.body: Arizona is missing its top three running backs and two of its receivers, and its starting quarterback situation is unsettled. The Rams' run defense ranks fourth in EPA allowed and its deep coverage second, so a patchwork offense has little room to get chunk plays. A shaky Arizona line also gives the weak Rams rush a rare chance to get home.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: Arizona allows touchdowns on most red-zone trips, one of the worst rates in the league. In Week 6 the Rams settled for 16 points. Converting drives into sevens is the difference between a cover and another close game.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers and special teams keep it close
waysToLose.body: This is how the Week 6 loss happened, and Arizona has won most of its one-score games. The Rams give the ball away regularly and now face a fill-in long snapper. A bad snap or a short-field touchdown hands a weak team the kind of tight game it has handled well.

waysToLose.title: Backup corners get exposed
waysToLose.body: With McDuffie and Watson out and little pass rush in front of them, the Rams' depth corners face their first real test. Arizona's receivers are depleted too. Still, coverage busts and soft slot play could hand a limited offense the explosive plays it can't create otherwise.

waysToLose.title: Stubbornly running into a good run defense
waysToLose.body: Arizona's defense is far better against the run than the pass. In the Week 6 loss the Rams' run game produced negative EPA. If Avila sits and the offense leans on the ground anyway, drives stall and the game stays low-scoring.

nextGame.watch: How often the Rams test their backup corners. If Arizona's patchwork offense can't find a weakness there, this is a comfortable win. If it can, the turnover and special teams problems make it another close game.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying team is good: top five in net EPA, an elite line and a defense that has carried it through an off year for the offense. Some of the record's drag should ease. Turnover margins and close-game results usually regress toward even, and the point differential already says this team is a win better than 5-4. What isn't luck is the injury list. A coverage-first defense without its top two corners, and a passing game that was already middling losing its lead receiver, are real downgrades until Nacua returns.

The schedule also cuts against a big finish. After Arizona come Green Bay and Kansas City at home, a trip to San Francisco and two games against a Seattle defense ranked fifth, with Dallas the only soft defense left. Expect a team that keeps games close and wins most of the coin flips it lost early, but not a run toward the division title against a San Francisco team at 7-1. A wild-card spot is the realistic target, and getting Nacua and the secondary back is what decides how comfortable that chase is.

confidence.note: Nine games of efficiency data and a stable QB, but major injuries at corner and receiver change the team that takes the field from here.
